extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, IP professionals, pharmaceutical and agrochemical industry stakeholders, and researchers interested in European SPC law
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for obtaining and calculating supplementary protection certificates (SPCs) in the European Economic Area: eligibility, scope, term calculation, extensions (including paediatric), relevant case law, and procedural/territorial issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of SPC
rubrics_metrics.description: A supplementary protection certificate (SPC) is a sui generis intellectual property (IP) right that extends the duration of certain rights associated with a patent. It enters into force after expiry of a patent upon which it is based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SPCs were introduced to compensate for time required to obtain regulatory approval (authorisation to put products on the market). They apply to certain regulated, biologically active agents (human/veterinary medicaments and plant protection products).

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligible subject-matter (medicinal and plant protection products)
rubrics_metrics.description: SPCs are available for various regulated, biologically active agents, namely human or veterinary medicaments and plant protection products (e.g. insecticides and herbicides).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SPCs extend the monopoly period for a 'product' defined as an active ingredient or a combination of active ingredients that is protected by a patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: SPC maximum term and combined exclusivity limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A supplementary protection certificate normally has a maximum lifetime of 5 years. The total combined duration of market exclusivity of a general patent and SPC cannot normally exceed 15 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The SPC term can be extended to 5.5 years for certain paediatric cases (see paediatric extension). The 6-month paediatric extension can extend combined patent+SPC exclusivity up to 15.5 years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paediatric extension (Article 36, Regulation 1901/2006)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 36 of Regulation 1901/2006 provides for a 6-month extension to SPC term. The extension is available only under certain conditions, the most notable being the requirement for the submission of a new MA application containing data from all trials conducted in accordance with an agreed Paediatric Investigation Plan (PIP).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: maximum SPC term up to 5.5 years; maximum market exclusivity (patent + SPC) up to at least 15.5 years. An extension can only be awarded if there is an SPC to extend; complex interactions arise when less than five years have elapsed between patent filing and MA issuance (see Models A/B/C and ECJ guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of SPC per Article 4
rubrics_metrics.description: According to Article 4 of Council Regulation (EEC) No 1768/92, the scope of an SPC extends 'only to the product covered by the authorization to place the corresponding medicinal product on the market and for any use of the product as a medicinal product that has been authorized before the expiry of the certificate'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limits protection to the product as authorised and to authorised uses up to the SPC expiry; interpretation disputes arise for multi-form or multi-ingredient products (see case law).

rubrics_metrics.name: ECJ interpretation: salts and derived forms (Case C-392/97)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Where an active ingredient in the form of a salt is referred to in the marketing authorisation concerned and is protected by a basic patent in force, the certificate is capable of covering the active ingredient as such and also its various derived forms such as salts and esters... in so far as they are covered by the protection of the basic patent."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ECJ case law can broaden the SPC scope beyond the exact physico-chemical form named in the MA where the patent's protection encompasses those derived forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal basis — governing EU regulations and EPC amendment
rubrics_metrics.description: SPCs in the EU are based primarily upon Council Regulation (EEC) No 1768/92 (recodified by Regulation (EC) No 469/2009) for medicinal products and Regulation (EC) No 1610/96 for plant protection products. Article 63 EPC was amended to permit Contracting States to extend the term of a European patent where regulatory authorisation is required before marketing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applications and rights are governed by these regulations and relevant EPC provisions; applicants must follow the statutory/regulatory framework and subsequent amendments (including paediatric and manufacturing-waiver regulations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacturing waiver (Regulation 2019/933)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation 2019/933 amended Reg. 469/2009 to introduce an 'SPC manufacturing waiver', allowing the manufacturing of SPC-protected products for the purpose of exporting them to third countries or of stockpiling them until expiry of the SPC (during the final 6 months of the SPC term), subject to safeguards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Safeguards include notification, export labeling/logo and other conditions; this is a derogation with specific procedural and substantive requirements that must be satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: SPC term calculation formula
rubrics_metrics.description: The term of an SPC depends on the date of issuance of the first marketing authorization (MA) within the EEA and can be determined by the equation: Term = date of 1st MA in the EEA − date of filing of corresponding patent − 5 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consequences: no SPC if less than 5 years elapsed between patent filing and 1st MA; if MA is >5 but <10 years after filing, SPC term is (elapsed − 5); if MA is >10 years after filing, SPC term is 5 years (maximum).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decisive MA date: regulatory authorisation date (Hässle AB, C-127/00)
rubrics_metrics.description: ECJ ruled that the decisive date for SPC purposes is the date of an authorisation from a regulatory body tasked with assessing safety and efficacy, and not the date of a subsequent authorisation required under national pricing or reimbursement provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent offices generally look to the safety/efficacy authorisation date; later national administrative acts (pricing, reimbursement) should not be used to delay SPC term calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralised MA date ambiguity (decision versus notification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Centralised (EMA/EC) marketing authorisations have two dates: (1) the date of the European Commission's decision to issue an authorisation, and (2) the date of notification of that decision to the MA applicant. There is disagreement whether date (1) or date (2) should be used for SPC term calculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some patent offices (e.g., UKIPO, Belgium) use date (2) (notification) to calculate SPC term, potentially lengthening SPCs slightly. Divergent national practices mean applicants should check local office practice or seek judicial clarification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-EEA MA treated as 1st MA in special circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: A marketing authorisation in Switzerland was considered as being a first MA for SPC calculation where that MA was automatically effective in Liechtenstein (an EEA member via treaty), per ECJ decisions (e.g., Novartis et al. and related cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Territorial/effectiveness nuances can affect which MA counts as 'first MA in the EEA'; treaty changes (e.g., post-2005 changes to Swiss-Liechtenstein arrangements) can change outcomes—applicants must consider cross-border effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: SPC availability conditions from ECJ (C-195/09 and C-427/09)
rubrics_metrics.description: ECJ cases C-195/09 and C-427/09 effectively ruled that SPCs for medicaments are only available for 'products' that: (a) are protected by a patent; (b) have been subject to an administrative authorisation procedure; and (c) have not been placed on the market anywhere in the EEA as a medicinal product prior to being subject to safety and efficacy testing and a regulatory review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tripartite test must be satisfied for SPC eligibility, but interpretation has been the subject of subsequent decisions and debate (see Neurim and Santen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of whether a 'product' is protected by the patent (claims test / Teva clarification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Case law (C-322/10 and C-422/10) indicated that the 'product' needs to be 'specified [or identified] in the wording of the claims'. The Teva decision (2018) clarified that for a product composed of several active ingredients, Article 3(a) requires that 'even if the combination of active ingredients ... is not expressly mentioned in the claims of the basic patent, those claims relate necessarily and specifically to that combination.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a product is 'protected by a patent' is a key, often controversial factual/legal inquiry—analysis of claim scope and whether claims necessarily and specifically relate to the product (including combinations) is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: One SPC per product / new-use exclusion (Santen decision)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Santen decision (2020) clarified that no SPC may be granted for a new use of a previously approved active ingredient, aligning with the traditional requirement of 'one SPC per product'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants seeking SPCs for second/novel therapeutic uses of known active ingredients should be aware that SPC protection is generally not available for mere new uses of previously approved active substances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction of prior marketing and SPC availability (Neurim and subsequent clarification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Neurim Pharmaceuticals (C-130/11) held that an SPC can be granted regardless of prior marketing of earlier veterinary products containing the product; however, this area is complex and later decisions (including Santen) narrowed certain possibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether prior marketing bars SPC protection depends on details (was prior MA subject to safety/efficacy testing consistent with legislation?) and evolving ECJ jurisprudence—national patent offices and courts may reach different conclusions absent clear ECJ guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of short intervals between patent filing and MA (Models A/B/C and national divergence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three models (A, B, C) were proposed for handling cases where less than five years elapsed between patent filing and first MA: Model A (allow zero or negative SPC terms, so extension can produce a positive term if >4.5 years), Model B (no SPC if ≤5 years), Model C (round negative terms up to zero, giving a minimum 6-month SPC after paediatric extension). National patent offices varied in approach until ECJ (C-125/10) essentially agreed with Model A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ECJ alignment with Model A means useful extended SPCs can be obtained so long as at least 4 years, 6 months and one day elapsed between filing and MA; practitioners should note historical divergence across member states and the possibility of litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: SPC application is national; no automatic EU-wide SPC
rubrics_metrics.description: Although all EU countries are required to provide SPCs, no unified cross-recognition exists. Applications must be filed and approved on a country-by-country basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must file SPC applications in each territory where protection is sought and comply with national patent office practices and interpretations (which may diverge).

rubrics_metrics.name: SPC enters into force only after corresponding patent expiry
rubrics_metrics.description: A supplementary protection certificate comes into force only after the corresponding general patent expires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The SPC is a post-patent expiry right that extends exclusivity; timing and expiry interplay between the basic patent and SPC is central to exclusivity strategy.
